prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 rows toward higher y, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
No trials have run yet. The starting network learned to end every episode with DONE at once: episode length fell to 1.0 by mid-training and dev success was 0. The traces explain why. The target height map in the observation is the true design rolled cyclically by Y/2 rows (observed row r = design row r+4, columns unchanged). Rewards and placements use the true frame. The starting network only sees a 5x5 neighbourhood, so it cannot match a target cell with the build cell 4 rows away. Placing without that information loses reward, and DONE (reward 0) wins. The build, missing and extra channels may also be rolled; I can't tell yet. So this round tests whether moving information across the grid fixes it. One candidate adds a fixed roll as a diagnostic. Two add learned global mixing, which handles any frame mix-up and should carry over to other grid sizes. All three use the same recipe: n_envs 128, so twice as many updates, and gamma 0.97.

### Round 2
The starting network and the two learned-mixing networks all collapsed to choosing DONE at once, or nearly so. The fixed half-roll network reached 0.89 (seeds 0.94 and 0.85). The diagnostic traces show why: the observed target is the true design shifted cyclically by Y/2 rows. Giving the network a copy of the input rolled back into line is what made learning possible; the learned full and axial mixing did not find the shift within the budget. The successful run is near-perfect but not complete: mean IoU 0.991 and 0.2 cells placed outside the target per episode. Its training success was still rising at the end (0.81 at 75%, 0.94 at 100%), so it looks short of samples. This round, each candidate makes one change to the r1c1 file: fewer PPO epochs to get more samples, a longer credit horizon so the +1 exact-build bonus counts for more, and a cheap global-context broadcast into the per-cell features.

### Round 3
The observed target is shifted by Y/2 rows. Rolling the input by Y//2 (r1c1) took the agent from always pressing DONE to 0.89 dev success (0.94 and 0.85 per seed). Learned remapping, full (r1c2) or axial (r1c3), did not find the shift within budget. On top of the roll, gamma 0.99 (0.85) and global broadcast (0.87) are within seed noise of 0.89, so neither helped. Two PPO epochs (0.66) gave one bad seed: more samples did not make up for less reuse per sample. With the roll, IoU is about 0.99 and training success was still rising at the end, so the limit is how well the agent learns per sample, not perception. Next tests: more gradient steps on the same samples (smaller minibatches), a higher learning rate, and a deeper trunk with a dilated convolution for larger receptive field, at the cost of fewer steps.

### Round 4
The observed target is shifted Y/2 rows away from the action frame. Without the half-roll input, training collapses to DONE. Learned mixing over cells (r1c2, r1c3) did not find the shift within the budget. With the roll, every variant scores between 0.85 and 0.89. These changes were r2c2 (gamma 0.99), r2c3 (global broadcast), r3c1 (32 minibatches) and r3c2 (lr 2e-3). r2c1 (2 epochs, 0.656) hurt, and r3c3 (a deeper net that cost samples, 0.738) hurt too. r1c1's 0.89 rests on one seed at 0.94 and one at 0.85, so its true mean is probably about 0.87. All variants show training success still rising at the end and IoU near 0.99, so the remaining failures are small errors in order or placement. The last round tests three cheap recipe changes that may speed late convergence without costing samples: lower entropy, 3 PPO epochs, and smaller, fresher updates.

## Trial it ended with
name: half-roll, ent_coef 0.003
hypothesis: Same as r1c1, with ent_coef cut from 0.01 to 0.003. The policy already places almost every cell correctly (IoU 0.99). The remaining failures are small order or placement errors, and the entropy bonus may slow commitment to the exact best action. Evaluation is greedy, so a sharper policy should help. Expect dev success above 0.89. A drop below 0.85, or a seed stuck early, would refute this by showing the bonus was needed for exploration.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).
